quiz_anat:1.q: With the body in anatomical position, the palms of the hands face in which direction?

quiz_anat:10.q: At which site on the anterior chest wall is the tricuspid valve best heard?
quiz_anat:10.r: APT M 2-2-5-5: tricuspid = 5th intercostal space, left sternal border.

quiz_anat:11.q: A murmur is loudest at the marked point (X). Blood passing through the valve best heard at this point has just left which structure?
quiz_anat:11.r: 2nd space right sternal border = aortic valve; aortic valve drains the left ventricle (p. 45).
quiz_anat:11.alt: Anterior chest wall with ribs and heart outlined and four colored points, one marked X

quiz_anat:12.q: Venae comitantes act as an arteriovenous pump. Which other function do they perform?
quiz_anat:12.r: Venae comitantes: arteriovenous pump + countercurrent heat exchanger.

quiz_anat:13.q: One artery supplying the knee is occluded, yet the tissue beyond it does not become ischemic. Which arrangement best explains this?

quiz_anat:14.q: Lymph from the left lower limb enters the venous circulation at which site?
quiz_anat:14.r: Thoracic duct drains everything except the right upper quadrant; empties at the left venous angle.

quiz_anat:15.q: When staging a carcinoma, surgeons remove and examine lymph nodes in a specific order. What determines that order?
quiz_anat:15.r: Nodal spread follows the natural routes of lymph drainage.

quiz_anat:16.q: Deep lymphatic vessels typically run alongside which structures?
quiz_anat:16.r: Deep lymph vessels accompany arteries; superficial ones follow the venous drainage.

quiz_anat:17.q: Pseudounipolar neurons have their cell bodies in which location?
quiz_anat:17.r: Pseudounipolar neurons sit in sensory ganglia, e.g. dorsal root ganglia.

quiz_anat:18.q: A collection of neuronal cell bodies located within the spinal cord is called a
quiz_anat:18.r: Nucleus = cell bodies in the CNS; ganglion = cell bodies in the PNS.

quiz_anat:19.q: Where does spinal nerve L3 leave the vertebral column?
quiz_anat:19.r: Only cervical nerves exit above their vertebra; all others exit below.

quiz_anat:2.q: A lesion in the left side of the brain causes weakness of the right arm. Relative to the lesion, the weakness is best described by which term?
quiz_anat:2.r: Contralateral = opposite side to the structure it is compared to.

quiz_anat:20.q: A lesion destroys only the structure at the marked point (X). Which deficit results in that spinal segment?
quiz_anat:20.r: X = dorsal root: afferent fibers only (SAME DAVE).
quiz_anat:20.alt: Cross-section diagram of the spinal cord and a spinal nerve with a point marked X

quiz_anat:23.q: Which structures are supplied by the dorsal ramus of a spinal nerve?
quiz_anat:23.r: Dorsal ramus: intrinsic back muscles + skin of the back; ventral ramus: everything else.

quiz_anat:24.q: Where are the cell bodies of preganglionic sympathetic neurons located?
quiz_anat:24.r: Sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies: lateral horn, T1-L2 only.

quiz_anat:25.q: A preganglionic sympathetic fiber passes through the sympathetic trunk without synapsing and continues to a prevertebral ganglion. What is this fiber's path called?
quiz_anat:25.r: Pathway 4: exit the trunk without synapsing as a splanchnic nerve.

quiz_anat:26.q: Which fibers travel in the gray rami communicantes?
quiz_anat:26.r: Gray rami = postganglionic 'off-ramps', entire trunk; white = preganglionic, T1-L2.

quiz_anat:27.q: Which effect results from parasympathetic activity?
quiz_anat:27.r: Parasympathetic: bronchoconstriction, pupil constriction, lower heart rate, coronary vasoconstriction.

quiz_anat:28.q: Which bone belongs to the axial skeleton?
quiz_anat:28.r: Axial: skull, hyoid, vertebrae, ribs, sternum, sacrum. Girdles are appendicular.

quiz_anat:29.q: A smooth, flat area covered with cartilage where one bone articulates with another is called a
quiz_anat:29.r: Facet = smooth flat cartilage-covered articular area; condyle = rounded knuckle-like.

quiz_anat:3.q: Which plane passes vertically through the body at right angles to the median plane?
quiz_anat:3.r: Frontal (coronal) plane: vertical, at right angles to the median plane; divides anterior from posterior.

quiz_anat:30.q: When a skeletal muscle shortens, one attachment is pulled toward the other. Which attachment moves?
quiz_anat:30.r: Origin = stationary bone; insertion = mobile bone; insertion is pulled toward origin.

quiz_anat:4.q: The image is an axial section of the thorax in standard radiologic orientation. Where in the patient does the marked point (X) lie?
quiz_anat:4.r: Axial image: top = anterior; image left = patient's right.
quiz_anat:4.alt: Axial CT section of the chest with a point marked X

quiz_anat:5.q: An axial computed tomography image is displayed as if the viewer is looking from which position?
o: From the head toward the feet
From the right toward the left
From the left toward the right
From the front toward the back
From the feet toward the head
quiz_anat:5.r: Axial images are viewed from the feet of a supine patient looking up.

quiz_anat:6.q: A standing patient bends the knee so that the heel moves toward the buttock. Which term describes this movement of the leg?
quiz_anat:6.r: Knee flexion moves the leg posteriorly (the exception).

quiz_anat:7.q: During pronation of the forearm, which bone pivots over which?
quiz_anat:7.r: Pronation: the radius pivots over the ulna.

quiz_anat:8.q: A patient turns the sole of the foot so that it faces inward. Which movement is this?
quiz_anat:8.r: Inversion = sole inward; eversion = sole outward.

quiz_anat:9.q: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood toward the heart?
quiz_anat:9.r: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from lungs to the left atrium.

quiz_anat_recheck:1.q: A seated patient straightens the knee, moving the leg anteriorly. Which movement is this?
quiz_anat_recheck:1.r: Knee: extension moves the leg anteriorly; flexion moves it posteriorly.

quiz_anat_recheck:10.q: Which effect results from sympathetic activity?
quiz_anat_recheck:10.r: Sympathetic: coronary vasodilation but systemic vasoconstriction.

quiz_anat_recheck:11.q: A sympathetic fiber travelling in a splanchnic nerve synapses in which type of ganglion?
quiz_anat_recheck:11.r: Splanchnic nerves leave the trunk unsynapsed and synapse in prevertebral ganglia.

quiz_anat_recheck:12.q: Which bone belongs to the axial skeleton?
quiz_anat_recheck:12.r: Axial: skull, hyoid, vertebrae, ribs, sternum, sacrum.

quiz_anat_recheck:2.q: A patient turns the sole of the foot so that it faces outward. Which movement is this?

quiz_anat_recheck:3.q: Lymph from the right upper limb enters the venous circulation at which site?
quiz_anat_recheck:3.r: Right lymphatic duct drains the right upper quadrant into the right venous angle.

quiz_anat_recheck:4.q: Superficial lymphatic vessels converge toward and follow which structures?
quiz_anat_recheck:4.r: Superficial lymph vessels follow the venous drainage; deep ones accompany arteries.

quiz_anat_recheck:5.q: A collection of neuronal cell bodies located outside the central nervous system is called a
quiz_anat_recheck:5.r: Ganglion = cell bodies in the PNS.

quiz_anat_recheck:8.q: The limbs and the anterior body wall are supplied by which part of a spinal nerve?
quiz_anat_recheck:8.r: Ventral ramus supplies everything except intrinsic back muscles and back skin.

quiz_anat_recheck:9.q: Which fibers travel in the white rami communicantes?
quiz_anat_recheck:9.r: White rami = preganglionic sympathetic on-ramps, T1-L2.

Anatomy High-Yield Tables (Exam 3)

Anatomy is 8 of the 81 questions on Exam 3, all from one lecture: Introduction to Gross Anatomy (Coker). Page numbers are pages of the combined PDF, where the lecture runs pp. 2–87. Everything is from the slides unless it is labeled (outside the slides).

1. Position, planes and axial images (LO 1–2)

All anatomical terms are expressed from anatomical position (p. 16).

Body part In anatomical position
Body Standing upright
Head Head and gaze directed forward
Upper limbs By the side, palms facing forward
Feet Planted, toes pointing forward
Plane Slide definition Also called Page
Median Vertical, through the midlines of head, neck and trunk; equal right and left sides Mid-sagittal 18
Sagittal Vertical, parallel to the median plane Para-sagittal 19
Frontal Vertical, at right angles to the median plane; anterior and posterior parts Coronal 20
Transverse Horizontal; superior and inferior parts Axial, cross-section 21

An axial image is read as if you stand at the feet of a supine patient and look toward the head (p. 22).

On the image Is the patient's
Top Anterior
Bottom Posterior
Left side Right
Right side Left

The labeled chest CT on p. 22 shows the ascending aorta and superior vena cava on the patient's right, and the pulmonary trunk and thoracic aorta on the patient's left. The esophagus sits just anterior to the vertebra.

2. Terms of relationship and laterality (LO 1)

Slides 24–29 show these pairs as labeled pictures with the synonyms. The one-line meanings are the standard definitions (outside the slides).

Pair Meaning Synonym on the slide Page
Superior / Inferior Toward the head / toward the feet Cranial / Caudal 24
Anterior / Posterior Front / back Ventral / Dorsal 25
Medial / Lateral Toward / away from the median plane 26
Proximal / Distal Nearer / farther from the limb's attachment 27
Superficial / Deep Nearer / farther from the surface 28
Palmar / Dorsal Palm / back of the hand 29
Plantar / Dorsal Sole / top of the foot 29
Laterality term Meaning Slide example (p. 30)
Bilateral Paired, right and left members Kidneys
Unilateral Found on one side only Liver
Ipsilateral Same side as the structure it is compared to Right arm and right leg
Contralateral Opposite side to the structure it is compared to Right eye and left eye

3. Terms of movement (LO 3)

Flexion moves the distal segment anteriorly at every joint on the slide except the knee (p. 33).

Joint Flexion moves Extension moves
Shoulder Arm anteriorly Arm posteriorly
Hip Thigh anteriorly Thigh posteriorly
Elbow Forearm anteriorly Forearm posteriorly
Knee Leg posteriorly Leg anteriorly
Movement Slide definition Page
Abduction Away from the midline ("abduct" = take away) 34
Adduction Toward the midline ("add" back to the body) 34
Medial (internal) rotation Turning the limb inward 35
Lateral (external) rotation Turning the limb outward 35
Pronation Internal rotation of forearm and hand; the radius pivots over the ulna 36
Supination External rotation of forearm and hand; the radius returns to anatomical position 36
Dorsiflexion Foot moves in the dorsal direction 37
Plantarflexion Foot moves in the plantar direction 37
Inversion Sole of the foot moves inward 37
Eversion Sole of the foot moves outward 37
Vertebral column movement Slide definition (p. 38)
Flexion Forward bending of the trunk
Extension Backward bending of the trunk
Lateral flexion Side bending to the left or right
Rotation Turning of the trunk or neck to the left or right

Abduction and adduction are pictured at the shoulder, the hip, and the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints (p. 34).

4. Heart: circuits, valves, flow, auscultation (LO 4)

The heart is two pumps in series; atria receive, ventricles pump away (pp. 42–43).

Circuit Leaves the heart from Via Blood leaving Returns via Returns to
Pulmonary Right ventricle Pulmonary arteries Deoxygenated Pulmonary veins (oxygenated) Left atrium
Systemic Left ventricle Systemic arteries Oxygenated Systemic veins (deoxygenated) Right atrium

The slide's rule: Arteries Always go Away from the heart, whatever the oxygen content (p. 43).

Valve Type Sits between Page
Tricuspid Atrioventricular Right atrium and right ventricle 44–45
Mitral (bicuspid) Atrioventricular Left atrium and left ventricle 44–45
Pulmonary Semilunar Right ventricle and pulmonary trunk 44–45
Aortic Semilunar Left ventricle and aorta 44–45

Blood flow through the heart (p. 45):

  1. Superior vena cava, inferior vena cava and coronary sinus
  2. Right atrium
  3. Tricuspid valve
  4. Right ventricle
  5. Pulmonary valve
  6. Pulmonary trunk, then pulmonary arteries, to the lungs
  7. Pulmonary veins
  8. Left atrium
  9. Mitral valve
  10. Left ventricle
  11. Aortic valve
  12. Aorta, to the body

Listen downstream from the flow of blood through each valve (p. 46). The slide's memory aid is "APT M, 2 2 5 5".

Valve Intercostal space Position
Aortic 2nd Right sternal border
Pulmonary 2nd Left sternal border
Tricuspid 5th Left sternal border
Mitral 5th Left midclavicular line

5. Blood vessels and vascular arrangements (LO 5)

Pressure sets wall thickness: high pressure gives arteries thick elastic walls, low pressure gives veins thin walls (p. 47).

Vessel Job Pressure and wall Typical blood Other features
Arteries Carry blood away from the heart; arterioles deliver it to capillaries High pressure, thick elastic walls Oxygen-rich
Capillaries Form capillary beds; exchange oxygen, nutrients and waste with extracellular fluid Site of exchange
Veins Venules drain the capillaries Low pressure, thin walls Low oxygen Valves, larger diameter
Arrangement What it is Why it matters Page
Anastomosis Communication between branches of arteries Collateral circulation: a blocked pathway does not cause ischemia or necrosis 48
Neurovascular bundle Artery, vein and nerve wrapped in deep (investing) fascia Fascia is connective tissue that envelops structures beneath the skin 48
Venae comitantes "Accompanying veins" that surround an artery in a branching network and share its fascial sheath Arteriovenous pump that drives venous blood toward the heart; countercurrent heat exchanger 48

The slide's example of an anastomosis is the genicular (knee) anastomosis (p. 48).

6. Lymphatic system (LO 6)

The lymphatic system is an "overflow" system: it returns excess tissue fluid and leaked plasma proteins to the bloodstream and removes debris from cellular decomposition and infection (p. 50). The functions listed on p. 49 are carrying lymph from the interstitial space to the venous system, filtering blood, and initiating an immune response.

Component Slide description (p. 50)
Lymph Tissue fluid that has entered lymph capillaries; usually clear, watery, slightly yellow
Lymphatic capillaries Thin-walled, blind-ended vessels among the blood capillaries; the entry point of the system
Lymphatic vessels Carry lymph from areas of collection to the venous system
Lymph nodes Small masses of lymph tissue along the vessels; filter lymph on its way to the venous system
Vessel group Location Receives from Page
Superficial Subcutaneous tissue; converge toward and follow the venous drainage 52
Deep Accompany arteries Superficial lymph vessels and internal organs 52

All lymph enters the venous circulation at the root of the neck (p. 52).

Duct Drains Empties at Formed by
Right lymphatic duct Right upper quadrant of the body Right venous angle Right internal jugular + right subclavian veins
Thoracic duct The remainder of the body Left venous angle Left internal jugular + left subclavian veins

Cancer (p. 53): lymphogenous spread is the most common route for the initial dissemination of carcinomas. Nodes trap the cells and become secondary (metastatic) sites. Involvement follows the natural drainage route, so surgeons stage by removing nodes in the order lymph passes through them.

7. Nervous system divisions and neurons (LO 7)

The nervous system is split two ways: by structure and by function (pp. 55–56).

Division Made of / carries
Central nervous system (CNS) Brain and spinal cord
Peripheral nervous system (PNS) Cranial nerves and spinal nerves
Afferent (sensory) Impulses from the periphery to the CNS
Efferent (motor) Impulses from the CNS to the periphery
Somatic Voluntary; CNS to skeletal muscle
Autonomic (ANS) Involuntary visceral motor; CNS to cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands
Sympathetic "Fight or flight"
Parasympathetic "Rest and digest"
Enteric Network of neurons in the wall of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract
Neuron term Slide definition (p. 57)
Nucleus Collection of neuronal cell bodies in the CNS
Ganglion Collection of neuronal cell bodies in the PNS
Dendrites Receive information
Axon Sends information
Multipolar neuron Most common type; in the CNS and the motor division of the PNS
Pseudounipolar neuron In sensory ganglia, such as dorsal root ganglia
Feature Cranial nerves Spinal nerves
Number 12 pairs 31 pairs
Origin The brain (mostly) Segmentally from the spinal cord
Route or naming Pass through openings in the skull Letter (C, T, L, S, Co) plus number

Numbering rule (p. 59): cervical nerves are numbered above the corresponding vertebra; all remaining nerves are numbered below it.

One nerve can carry fibers with different functions. The phrenic nerve is motor to the diaphragm and sensory to the fibrous pericardium and parietal pleura (p. 58).

8. Spinal nerve, dermatomes and myotomes (LO 8)

Roots are split by direction; rami are split by territory and each carries all four fiber types (pp. 60–61).

Part Carries Detail
Dorsal root Afferent only: somatic afferent and visceral afferent Carries the dorsal root ganglion (DRG); afferent information arrives at the dorsal horn
Ventral root Efferent only: somatic efferent and visceral efferent Efferent information exits from the ventral horn
Spinal nerve Mixed Formed where the two roots join
Dorsal ramus Mixed Intrinsic back muscles and skin of the back
Ventral ramus Mixed Everything else
Ramus communicans Sympathetic fibers Link to the sympathetic ganglion and chain

The slide's memory aid is SAME DAVE: Sensory Afferent, Motor Efferent; Dorsal Afferent, Ventral Efferent (p. 61).

Term Definition Tested by Page
Dermatome Area of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve Touch 62
Myotome Portion of skeletal muscle innervated by a single spinal nerve Reflex 62–63
Dermatome Landmark labeled on p. 62
C3 Front of the neck
C8 Ring and little fingers
T4 Nipples
T10 Umbilicus
L1 Inguinal region
L4 Knee
L5 Anterior ankle and foot
Reflex Spinal levels (p. 63)
Biceps C5, C6
Brachioradialis C5, C6
Triceps C7, C8
Quadriceps L3, L4
Achilles S1, S2

The slide's myotome example: the femoral nerve (L2–L4) supplies quadriceps femoris, and knee extension tests L3 and L4 (p. 63).

9. Somatic vs autonomic; sympathetic vs parasympathetic (LO 9)

The autonomic nervous system (ANS) is a two-neuron motor system: a pre-ganglionic neuron, a ganglion, then a post-ganglionic neuron to the effector (p. 67).

Feature Somatic Autonomic
Supplies All parts of the body except viscera, smooth muscle and glands Viscera, smooth muscle and glands
Sensory side Touch, temperature, pain from the periphery
Motor target Skeletal muscle Cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, glands
Page 64 65
Feature Sympathetic Parasympathetic Page
Outflow Thoraco-lumbar: lateral horn, T1–L2 Cranial-sacral: cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and S2–S4 70–71, 78
Pre-ganglionic fiber Short Long 70
Post-ganglionic fiber Long Short 70
Ganglia Sympathetic trunk or prevertebral Cranial or intramural 70, 72, 78
Pupil Dilation Constriction 66
Heart rate Increases Decreases 66
Coronary vessels Vasodilation Vasoconstriction 66
Bronchi Bronchodilation Bronchoconstriction 66
GI tract Inhibits activity Stimulates; intestinal vasodilation 66
Other Systemic vasoconstriction, sweating Salivation, lacrimation 66
Ganglion type Location Slide example (pp. 67–68)
Paravertebral Close to the spinal cord Sympathetic trunk
Prevertebral Along the midline in the abdomen Celiac, superior mesenteric
Intrinsic (intramural) On or within the organ innervated GI tract, heart
Cranial In the head, with cranial nerves "COPS" ganglia

COPS is not spelled out on the slide: ciliary, otic, pterygopalatine, submandibular (outside the slides).

Ramus communicans Fibers Slide nickname Found at Page
White Pre-ganglionic "On-ramps" T1–L2 only 69
Gray Post-ganglionic "Off-ramps" Entire trunk 69

Every sympathetic pre-ganglionic fiber starts the same way: lateral horn, ventral root, spinal nerve, white ramus communicans, sympathetic trunk. It then takes one of four paths (pp. 73–77):

  1. Synapse at the level of entry
  2. Ascend the trunk, then synapse
  3. Descend the trunk, then synapse
  4. Exit the trunk without synapsing there, as a splanchnic nerve, and synapse in a prevertebral ganglion

The prevertebral ganglia named on p. 72 are the celiac, superior mesenteric, aorticorenal and inferior mesenteric. The trunk ganglia are cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral and the ganglion impar.

10. Skeleton, bone markings, joints and muscle (LO 10)

Skeletal muscle shortens and pulls its insertion toward its origin (p. 85).

Skeleton Bones (p. 80)
Axial Head (skull); neck (hyoid, cervical vertebrae); trunk (ribs, sternum, vertebrae, sacrum)
Appendicular Limbs, including the pectoral and pelvic girdles
Limb segment Runs between Compartments Bones Page
Shoulder Proximal segment; overlaps trunk and neck Pectoral, scapular and deltoid regions 81
Arm Shoulder to elbow Anterior, posterior Humerus 81
Forearm Elbow to wrist Anterior, posterior Radius, ulna 81
Hand Distal segment Carpals, metacarpals, phalanges 81
Gluteal region Transition between trunk and free lower limb 82
Thigh Gluteal, abdominal and perineal regions to knee Anterior, posterior, medial Femur 82
Leg Knee to ankle Anterior, posterior, lateral Tibia, fibula 82
Foot Distal part Tarsals, metatarsals, phalanges 82
Bone marking Slide definition (p. 83)
Body Principal mass
Crest Ridge
Process Projection or outgrowth
Notch Indentation
Fossa Shallow depression
Foramen Opening or hole
Facet Smooth flat area covered in cartilage for articulation with another bone
Condyle Rounded knuckle-like articular area
Epicondyle Eminence superior or adjacent to a condyle
Trochanter Projections of the proximal femur
Tubercle Small rounded projection
Tuberosity Roughened elevation
Synovial joint Axes Movements (p. 84)
Ball-and-socket Multiaxial Flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, rotation, circumduction
Hinge Uniaxial Flexion/extension
Muscle term Slide definition (p. 85)
Fleshy portion Contractile, striated muscle
Tendon Noncontractile; the means of attachment
Origin Attachment on the stationary bone
Insertion Attachment on the mobile bone

11. Word roots, eponyms and course terms

These come from the "learn the language" slides and are not tied to a numbered learning objective, so treat them as lower yield.

Root Meaning Slide examples Page
gaster Stomach, belly Esophagogastric junction, epigastric region, digastric muscle 10
rectus Straight Rectus abdominis, vasa recta, rectus femoris 11
-oid Like, resemblance to Cuboid, deltoid, mastoid 12
-ceps, capitis (from caput) Head Biceps brachii, quadriceps femoris, caput medusae, splenius capitis 13
Eponym Descriptive name (p. 14)
Adam's apple Laryngeal prominence
Alcock canal Pudendal canal
Auerbach plexus Myenteric plexus
Bartholin gland Greater vestibular gland
Buck fascia Deep fascia of the penis
Cooper ligament Suspensory ligament of the breast
Pouch of Douglas Rectouterine pouch
Eustachian tube Pharyngotympanic tube
Fallopian tube Uterine tube
Gerota fascia Renal fascia
Guyon canal Ulnar canal
Loop of Henle Nephron loop
Hesselbach triangle Inguinal triangle
Bundle of His Atrioventricular bundle
Hunter canal Adductor canal
Angle of Louis Sternal angle
Meckel diverticulum Ileal diverticulum
Morrison pouch Hepatorenal recess
Ligament of Treitz Suspensory ligament of the duodenum
Ampulla of Vater Hepatopancreatic ampulla
Wharton duct Submandibular duct
Circle of Willis Cerebral arterial circle
Wirsung duct Main pancreatic duct
Term Slide definition Page
Anatomy Study of the structure of the body; from Greek temnein, "to cut" 5–6
Histology Microscopic anatomy 6
Gross anatomy Macroscopic anatomy 6
Embryology Study of the formation and development of an embryo and fetus 6
Physiology Study of the function of body structures 6
Systemic approach Pictured only on the slide; studied one body system at a time (outside the slides) 6–7
Regional approach Each region studied separately, all aspects at once; emphasis on relationships 8

12. Pairs you are likely to swap

You tend to swap paired terms, so these are the ones to say out loud before the exam.

Pair Keep straight Page
Knee vs other joints Knee flexion moves the leg posteriorly; shoulder, hip and elbow flexion move anteriorly 33
Aortic vs pulmonary listening post Aortic is right of the sternum, pulmonary is left; both 2nd space 46
Tricuspid vs mitral listening post Tricuspid is left sternal border, mitral is left midclavicular line; both 5th space 46
Pulmonary arteries vs veins Arteries carry deoxygenated blood away; veins carry oxygenated blood back 43
Right lymphatic vs thoracic duct Right duct drains only the right upper quadrant; thoracic duct drains the rest, into the left venous angle 52
Nucleus vs ganglion Nucleus is in the CNS; ganglion is in the PNS 57
Dorsal root vs dorsal ramus Root is afferent only; ramus is mixed and goes to the back 60–61
White vs gray rami White is pre-ganglionic, T1–L2; gray is post-ganglionic, entire trunk 69
Sympathetic vs parasympathetic fibers Sympathetic: short pre, long post. Parasympathetic: long pre, short post 70
Coronary vs systemic vessels Sympathetic dilates coronary vessels but constricts systemic vessels 66
Dermatome vs myotome Dermatome is skin, tested by touch; myotome is muscle, tested by reflex 62–63
Cervical vs other spinal nerves Cervical exit above their vertebra; the rest exit below 59
Origin vs insertion Origin is the stationary bone; insertion is the mobile bone 85
Pronation vs supination In pronation the radius pivots over the ulna; supination returns it 36
Inversion vs eversion Inversion turns the sole inward; eversion turns it outward 37
Axial image sides The patient's right is on the left of the image 22
Thigh vs leg compartments Thigh: anterior, posterior, medial. Leg: anterior, posterior, lateral 82
